messages.subject: Correcting effort on coastal line transects with habitat on only part of one side
messages.subject_clean: Correcting effort on coastal line transects with habitat on only part of one side
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am helping with a distance sampling analysis of two forest bird species on a small island. Four of the 19 transects (about 13 of 46 km of effort, roughly 10% of detections) follow a coastal road. Distances are measured from the road edge and are folded. On the inland side, forest extends beyond the truncation distance w. On the sea side, habitat only extends from the road edge up to 5 to 20 m depending on the transect.

How would you handle this kind of data?

One suggestion we received was that the expected number of detections on such a transect could be written as D·L·(μ + ∫₀ʰ g(x)dx) instead of D·2L·μ, where h is the width of available habitat on the sea side. The coastal transects could therefore be handled as follows:
fit g(x) on the 15 non-coastal transects only
use this g(x) to multiply the effort of the coastal transects by (μ + ∫₀ʰ g(x)dx) / 2μ;
include the coastal detections in the encounter rate only, without using their distances in the detection function fit;
propagate the uncertainty in g(x) into the corrected effort with a bootstrap over transects.
So far, we have only applied steps 1 and 2, then refitted the model on all 19 transects with the corrected effort. This increases abundance by 8 to 12%. Average p barely differs with or without the coastal transects (0.606 vs 0.615 and 0.612 vs 0.618 for the two species).

Before we continue, I have a couple of questions:
Is this a defensible approach, and is there a reference for something similar?
Is refitting on all 19 transects acceptable given the small difference in p, or is there a recommended way to implement step 3?
Is there anything else we should be aware of?

Thanks in advance for your advice.

Dear all,

Join our online course “Design, Implement and Promote Species Monitoring in R”, taking place 19–21 October.

Course website: https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/species-monitoring-in-r/

Designed for researchers, students, practitioners and NGO professionals, this practical course will help you develop robust, reproducible species monitoring protocols and analyse real-world data in R.

You will explore and apply key monitoring approaches, including:
Capture-Mark-Recapture (CMR)
Distance sampling

Previous basic experience with R is desirable, but all scripts will be provided and explained step by step.

Carlo

messages.subject: Re: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.subject_clean: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.body_plain:
Dear James,

I think your approach of pre-processing the data to left-truncate where there is a restricted view from the plane and subtract this distance from the remaining distances is appropriate. This allows you to combine the data from the two planes. The assumption you are then making (assuming a single-platform analysis) is that you are detecting everything at that left-truncation distance, as if it were on the transect. One suggestion I have is to use plane as a covariate in the detection function model. You have not said if the two planes were surveying across a single area of interest or whether there was any stratification? That suggestion is particularly important if there is stratification present and the planes were surveying different strata and you want estimates at the stratum level.

I do not think left-truncation of the data from both planes would be appropriate as the other plane looks like g(0) will be less than 1 at that distance and it also looks like it would create a more spiked detection function.

Best wishes,
Laura

Laura Marshall
Distance Development Team

On Friday, 11 September 2026 at 16:46:17 UTC+1 hods...@gmail.com wrote:
> Good morning,
> I am working on analysis of an aerial transect distance-sampling survey for moose in the Northwest Territories.  I was hoping to get some feedback on the approach I used to deal with different blind spots between aircraft to see if it makes sense or violates any model assumptions. The survey used two different aircraft, one was a Cessna 180 and the other was a Found Bush Hawk.  The Bush Hawk has bubble windows on all four doors which extend down almost to the floor.  When I plotted our detection distances by aircraft I found that the Bush Hawk didn't really have a blind spot under the plane, whereas the Cessna 180 seemed to have blind spot out to 150 m:
>
> To address this I filtered out observations <150 m from the Cessna (FUGR).  I also filtered out observations >650 m for the Bush Hawk, and greater than 800 m for the Cessna.  This was to ensure that I was using observations from an equal strip width for each plane (650 m wide).  I then subtracted 150 m from the remaining Cessna observation detection distances.  This approach retained 139 of the 151 original moose observations.  It yielded the following adjusted histogram (each aircraft separately, and the combined histogram for both aircraft below it):
>
> I then fit Half Normal and Hazard Rate models without adjustment terms to the data.  The fit of both models was pretty decent, but the Half Normal model performed slightly better based on AIC:
> AIC -167.90
> Distance sampling Cramer-von Mises test (unweighted)
> Test statistic = 0.0445782 p-value = 0.908257
> Abundance Estimate: 1804 (cv 0.17)
> AIC -166.99
> Distance sampling Cramer-von Mises test (unweighted)
> Test statistic = 0.0481351 p-value = 0.887509
> Abundance estimate: 1677 (cv 0.18)
>
> I also tried models with left and right data truncation for both aircraft. Data was left truncated at 200 m and right truncated at 800 m, retaining 96 of the 151 moose observations.  The Half Normal model fit the truncated data well (CvM p-value = 0.96), but the abundance estimate was much higher (N=2977 and cv = 0.21).  The Hazard Rate model with the same truncation did not fit quite as well (CvM p-value  = 0.78) but yielded an estimate a bit closer to my approach outlined above (N = 1851 and cv = 0.2).
>
> Any advice on which approach might be best to use would be much appreciated!
>
> Thanks
>

messages.subject: Help to understand results
messages.body_plain:
Warm greetings,

I hope you are doing well. My name is Santiago Hernández, I'm a biology student in La Universidad de La Salle de Colombia.
I contacted Eric last year for advice and help interpreting some Distance data. I see that he is no longer at St Andrews, so I am reaching out to you; I really hope you can help, as I haven't been able to make much progress on my thesis project due to not fully understanding the results.

I’ve had to pause my project on the population density of *Cistothorus apolinari*; there have been some fires here in Colombia that required attention, and work commitments also forced me to postpone the research. However, I have now decided to resume the project, with the aim of providing tools for the conservation of this bird and the Andean *páramos*.

I shared the data in zip file. I would appreciate it if you could review them and share your thoughts. Based on the AIC values and the number of parameters, I identified analysis number 10 as the best model. However, I have a few questions regarding the "Expected cluster size" and "Density & abundance" windows. Is the average cluster size calculated per count point or for the entire sampled area? The same applies to the population density estimates: do the populations in the Laguna de Socha and Peña Negra sectors consist of 23 and 36 individuals, respectively? Does *Distance* provide a final density estimate for just a single sampling point or for the entire sampled area? Does the final value we see represent the total number of individuals in the entire area?

Thank you in advance for your patience and for taking the time to read this. It would be a great help if you were willing to collaborate, though I also understand that you have other responsibilities, so I completely understand if you are unable to reply.

Thanks again, and I hope we stay in touch. Best regards from Colombia.
P.S.: I look forward to the next Distance course so I can participate.

messages.subject: Re: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.subject_clean: Aircraft-specific truncation to address different blind spots
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura,
Thank you very much for your response!   I have included aircraft as a covariate in subsequent models using the aircraft-specific truncation and it did come out as my top model.  The Cessna was estimated to have a lower detection probability overall than the other aircraft (see plot below). The survey area was split into two strata, and both planes surveyed transects within each stratum.  The lower detection of the Cessna could have been luck of the draw in terms of which areas it surveyed, or a result of observer acuity.  Unfortunately we had a lot of turnover in observers during the survey so I was not able to test the effect of different observer pairs directly.
Cheers,
James
